title: The Snares
body:
Tomas is ten years old. He has no mother and no father. He lives in a monastery in the mountains, the monastery of Saint Ansel. Many monks live there, and twelve children live there too. The children are all orphans, like Tomas.

Tomas has two friends. Bram is eleven. He is the oldest boy in the monastery. He is tall and loud, and he likes to tell the other children what to do. Pip is eight. He is small and funny, and he talks all day. He talks to birds, to trees and to animals.

Tomas is different. He is quiet. He does not talk much, but he looks at everything and he thinks a lot.

In spring the food in the monastery is not good. Every day there is only bread and a little soup. The boys are always hungry.

It is early in the morning, and the monks are still asleep. The three boys climb over the wall and go into the forest. This is not allowed. The abbot, Father Gerard, says it every week: “No children in the forest!” But the boys want meat.

In the forest the boys have snares. A snare is a small trap for rabbits. Tomas makes very good snares.

“Be quiet!” says Bram. But Bram is the loudest of the three.

The first snare is empty. Tomas sees some grey hair on the rope. “There was a rabbit here,” he says. “But it is gone.”

“Your snare is bad,” says Bram.

Tomas does not answer. His snare is not bad. He makes the knot stronger and puts the snare a little lower.

In the second snare there is a rabbit. Bram takes it, and he is very happy. “I have a rabbit!” he says. But it is Tomas's snare, not Bram's.

On the way home, Pip stops. On an old tree there is a grey rabbit with a torn ear. It looks at the boys. It is not afraid.

“Look! That is the rabbit from the first snare,” says Pip. “He is very clever. His name is the King.”

Near an old path, Tomas stops again. On the ground he sees the marks of horses. They are big and new. Who has big horses here? Only rich men. Tomas looks at the marks for a long time, but he says nothing to Bram and Pip.

Brother Anselm is at the gate of the monastery. He is an old monk, very kind. He knows: the boys were in the forest.

The boys must copy a page from an old book. It is the story of an emperor. “His blood came down from the stars,” says the book.

“It is only a story,” says Bram.

Brother Anselm smiles. “Many things are only stories,” he says. “Until one day they are not.”

title: Thieves in the Night
body:
It is night. Everybody in the monastery is asleep. Only Tomas is awake. He thinks about the horse marks in the forest. Who comes to a monastery on big horses? Maybe the men want to come back at night, he thinks.

Then he hears a noise outside. He goes to the window. The moon is big and bright. In the yard there are four men. They go to the chapel. In the chapel the monks have two beautiful things: an old silver cup and a small gold box. These things are very old and very expensive.

“Thieves!” thinks Tomas.

The monks are good men, but they cannot fight. And Tomas cannot fight four men. He can shout, but then the thieves run away with the silver. He needs a plan.

He wakes Bram. “Bram, listen,” he says quietly. “Go up the bell tower. I knock on the wall two times, and then you ring the bell. Ring it very loud!”

Bram wants to say something. He does not like orders from Tomas. But he looks at Tomas's face, and he goes.

Pip wakes up too. He sees the men in the yard and he is very afraid. He hides under a bench, and he stays there all night.

Tomas takes his rope for the snares and runs down the stairs to the cellar. The cellar has a door to the forest. The thieves want to go out this way, he thinks. On the third stair he ties the rope from one wall to the other. It is low and tight, like a snare for rabbits.

Then he knocks on the wall. One, two.

The bell rings. It is very, very loud. The monks wake up, and there are lights in all the windows. The thieves are afraid. They run to the cellar with the silver. The first thief does not see the rope. He falls down the stairs and he cries out. His leg is broken. The other thieves drop the cup and the box, and they run into the forest.

Tomas goes back up to the window. Near the trees he sees a fifth man. The man does not run. He is not with the thieves. He only looks at the windows of the children's bedroom. He has only one eye. Is he counting the children?

In the morning, everybody talks about the night. “The bell is my idea,” says Bram, and the monks say Bram is a hero. Tomas says nothing. For him that is OK.

But he does not tell anybody about the man with one eye.

title: Counting Heads
body:
After the night of the thieves, the monastery is quiet again. The lord's men come and take the thief with the broken leg to the castle. “Now everything is OK,” they say. The abbot is happy. “God looks after our home,” he says, and he says thank you to Bram for the bell.

One week later, a man comes to the monastery. He buys and sells wool. He has two big wagons, four horses and a servant. He is very nice. He has good clothes and he speaks politely. He buys the wool of the monastery for a good price, and he gives the monks a big barrel of wine.

The man has only one eye. On the other eye he has a black patch.

Tomas sees him, and he knows: that is the man from the night.

The trader wants to leave the next day, but he does not leave. One day his wagon has a broken wheel. The next day it rains. And the man is always near the children. He asks the young monks a lot of questions. “How many children live here? How old are they? Do they go to the forest alone?”

Tomas goes to the abbot. “Father, that man was here on the night of the thieves,” he says. “I saw him near the forest.”

The abbot looks at him. He is kind, but he does not believe Tomas. “It was night, Tomas, and it was dark. Now you see a man with one eye, and you think: that is the man. No. We do not judge a man by his face.”

Bram laughs at Tomas. “You want to be a hero, like me,” he says.

Pip has a new friend: the trader. Every afternoon the man gives Pip a honey cake, and Pip goes everywhere with him, like a little dog. “He is very nice,” says Pip. “He asks me about our snares in the forest, and I show him the snares.”

On the third day the trader leaves. He smiles and waves from his wagon. In the evening nobody talks about him, and soon everybody forgets him.

But Tomas does not forget. At night he goes to the kitchen. He takes a small knife and a long rope for snares. He puts the knife and the rope under his shirt. From this day he always has them with him. Every day. Every night.

title: Pip the Mouse
body:
The trader is gone, but the children still talk about the night of the thieves. And they laugh at Pip. “Pip the mouse!” they say. “Where is the mouse? Under the bench!” Pip laughs too, but at night he is sad. In his bed he cries a little. Tomas hears him, but he says nothing.

Pip is not like Tomas or Bram. He is small, and he is afraid of many things: the dark, big dogs, deep water. But he is never afraid of people. He likes everybody, and everybody likes him. The cook gives him bread with butter. The old monks tell him stories. The little children go everywhere with him.

One morning Pip comes to Tomas. “Tomas, I want to learn,” he says. “Teach me the snares. Teach me the knots. I don't want to be a mouse.”

Tomas looks at him. Then he takes a piece of rope from under his shirt. “OK,” he says. “Sit down.”

They sit behind the barn, in the sun. Tomas makes a knot, very slowly. “Now you,” he says.

Pip tries. His fingers are small, and the rope does not listen to him. The knot is bad. He tries again. And again. Tomas does not laugh. He only says: “Again.”

After one hour, Pip's knot is good. After three days, it is very good.

“A good knot is strong,” says Tomas. “But every knot can open. You only need to know where to pull.” He shows Pip the place. Pip pulls, and the knot opens.

Now Pip has a new game. Tomas makes a knot, and Pip opens it. Every day he is faster. On the fifth day he opens Tomas's best knot in two seconds. “I am faster than you!” he says, and he laughs and laughs. “This is my knot now. It is the King's knot.”

In the evening the two boys sit on the wall and look at the mountains. Pip talks, like always.

“Tomas, do you know your mother?”

“No.”

“Me too. The monks say I was in a basket at the gate. It was winter, and it was very cold. In the basket there was a baby and a little bird of wood. Only that. No name. The monks call me Pip, because I am so small.” He takes the wooden bird from his pocket. “This is from my mother, I think.”

“I was at the gate too,” says Tomas.

“Do you think about your mother?”

“No,” says Tomas. But that is not true. He thinks about her very often.

Pip puts his head on Tomas's shoulder. “Then we are brothers,” he says. “OK?”

Tomas is quiet for a long time. Then he says: “OK.”

title: The River
body:
Summer comes, and the days are hot. Every Saturday the monks take the children to the river. The children wash the clothes of the monastery, and after the work they can swim.

The big boys jump into the water from a rock. Bram jumps first, of course. “Look at me!” he shouts. The little children play near the bank.

Only Pip does not go into the water. He sits on the grass and watches.

“Pip, come in!” says Bram. “Or is the mouse afraid of water?” The other children laugh.

Pip smiles, but his face is red. He cannot swim. And here the river is deep and fast.

Tomas gets out of the water and sits next to Pip. “Come with me,” he says.

They walk up the river. Here the water is slow and not deep. It only comes to Pip's stomach. Nobody can see them.

“I can teach you,” says Tomas. “Like the knots.”

Pip goes into the water, very slowly. It is cold. Tomas holds him. “Put your head back. Put your arms out. Now lie on the water.”

Pip tries, but then he is afraid. He moves his arms and legs very fast, and he drinks a lot of water. He stands up and coughs. “I can't,” he says. “The water wants to eat me.”

“Again,” says Tomas.

Pip looks at him. Then he lies on the water again. This time Tomas does not let him go. For a few seconds Pip lies on the river like a leaf. “I can do it!” he shouts, and he goes under again.

They come back to this place every Saturday. Pip learns a little, but only a little. He can lie on the water, but he cannot swim. “Next summer,” he says. “Next summer I can swim like a fish.”

On the bank, the little children are tired, and they want a story. Pip always has a story for them. Today it is about the King. “The King lives under the old oak,” he says. “He has a crown of grass, and he is very clever. Nobody can catch him. Not Bram, not the abbot, not even Tomas!” The little children laugh. They love the King.

On the way home Pip walks next to Tomas.

“Tomas, are you afraid sometimes?”

Tomas thinks about the man with one eye. “Yes,” he says. “Every day.”

Pip stops. “You? Really?”

“Really.”

Pip thinks about this for a long time. Then he takes Tomas's hand, and they walk home together.

That evening Tomas goes to his snares alone. Near the first snare there are marks on the ground. They are not from rabbits, and they are not from horses. They are from big boots. Somebody was here, at his snares.

title: Taken
body:
It is a warm day at the end of summer. The monks send eight children into the forest for firewood. “Come back before dark,” says the abbot.

The little children collect wood near the path. Tomas, Bram and Pip go a little further, to the snares. Pip has a honey cake in his hand. The trader gave him a big bag of honey cakes.

The forest is very quiet. Tomas stops.

“Listen,” he says.

“I don't hear anything,” says Bram.

“Yes. That is the problem. The birds are quiet.”

Then the men come out of the trees. There are five men, with big boots and long knives, and two big dogs. The little children scream and run, but the men are faster. They catch the children one by one, like rabbits.

Tomas does not run. He takes his knife from under his shirt. A man comes to him, and Tomas cuts his arm. The man shouts. Then another man hits Tomas on the head. Tomas falls, and for a moment everything is dark.

He opens his eyes. His face is on the ground. A man takes his knife and his rope.

Bram stands near the snares. He is the oldest and the tallest. Every day he tells the other children what to do. But now he does not move. He does not fight, and he does not run. He only cries. “Mother!” he cries. “Mother!” But Bram has no mother. He never had a mother.

Pip is under the arm of a big man. He kicks and kicks, but he is very small. His honey cake falls on the ground.

The men tie the children's hands with rope. On the path there is a big wagon, and on the wagon there is a cage of wood. The men put the eight children in the cage. They close the door with a thick rope and a big knot.

Then a man comes on a horse. He has a black patch on one eye. He looks into the cage and counts the children. “Eight,” he says. “Good.”

Pip looks at him with big eyes. It is the trader, the nice man with the honey cakes.

“Where are we going?” asks Pip.

The man smiles. “To the sea, little one. In the towns by the sea there are ships, and there are people with money. They buy children.”

The wagon starts. It goes south, away from the mountains, away from the monastery.

In the evening the children are not home. The monks take lights and go into the forest. They call and call, but nobody answers. They find the snares. The snares are empty. On the ground there is only a honey cake.

title: The Cage Wagon
body:
The wagon goes south for many days. The road is long and bad, and the wagon is slow. In the cage there is not much room. The children sit on old straw. It rains, and they are wet.

Every morning the men give them a little bread and some water. Only a little. The children are always hungry.

Bram is not the old Bram now. He does not give orders. He does not talk much. At night he cries, and the little children look at him with big eyes. The oldest boy is crying, so everything is very bad, they think.

Pip sits next to Bram and holds his hand. “It's OK, Bram,” he says. “It's OK.” Then he looks at the little children. “Do you want a story?”

“Yes!”

“One day some bad men come to the forest, with dogs and with nets. They want to catch the King. But the King runs under the old oak, and the dogs cannot find him. Nobody can catch the King. Nobody!”

The little children laugh a little. Every evening they want a new story about the King, and every evening Pip has one.

Tomas does not tell stories. But he watches everything.

There are five men. Two men drive the wagon, and two men ride next to it. The man with one eye rides at the front. He is the boss, and the men call him Odo. There are two dogs too. At night one man is always awake and watches the cage. First the young man with red hair, then the fat man, then the old man. The old man drinks a lot of wine, and he often sleeps. Tomas remembers all of this.

Tomas looks at the door of the cage. The knot is big, but it is not a good knot. Every knot can open. You only need to know where to pull. But Tomas cannot reach it from inside the cage.

Every day Tomas eats only half of his bread. He hides the other half under the straw. In the wagon there are old pieces of rope. Tomas takes them one by one, and he hides them under his shirt.

He has a plan, but he tells nobody. Bram is not strong now. Maybe he cries and says something to the men. And Pip talks all day. A plan in Pip's mouth is not a secret for long.

“Tomas, what are you thinking?” asks Pip one evening.

“Nothing,” says Tomas.

“You always think something. I know you.”

“Sleep, Pip.”

Pip takes the wooden bird from his pocket. “The bird says we go home soon,” he says quietly. He puts his head on Tomas's shoulder, and he sleeps.

Tomas does not sleep. He watches the knot on the door.

title: Pip
body:
On the seventh day the wagon comes to a big river. There is no bridge. The water is brown, deep and fast. The men stop. They want to find a good place to cross.

The men take the horses to the water. The horses drink. Only the old man stays near the cage, and soon he is asleep.

Pip looks at the door of the cage. The knot is not tight today. It is loose.

“Tomas,” he says quietly. “Look. The knot.”

“I see it,” says Tomas. “Wait.”

But Pip does not want to wait. Seven days in a cage is a long time. He is tired and hungry, and he does not want to be the mouse. Today he wants to be like Tomas.

Pip is the smallest of all the children. He puts his head between the bars of the cage, then one shoulder, then the other. And then he is outside.

“Pip, no!” says Tomas. But it is too late.

Pip goes to the door. His small fingers are on the knot. It is the King's knot, and he knows where to pull. The knot is almost open.

Then a dog barks. The young man with red hair turns around. “Hey!” he shouts, and he runs to the wagon.

Pip runs along the bank of the river. He is fast, but the man is faster. The man catches Pip by his shirt. Pip kicks and fights like a little cat. Then the man falls, and Pip falls with him into the river.

Here the water only comes to the man's stomach. But the river takes Pip away from the bank, into the deep water. Pip cannot swim. Tomas sees his head once. Then there is only brown water.

Tomas holds the bars of the cage and looks at the river. Pip does not come up.

Odo comes. He is very angry, but not because of Pip. Because of the money. “One child less,” he says. Then the men beat the children with sticks. All of them, the little ones too. The men tie the door again, with a new rope and three knots.

Tomas does not cry. He does not feel anything. On the floor of the cage there is something small. It is Pip's wooden bird. Tomas takes it and holds it in his hand.

At night Tomas does not sleep. It is my fault, he thinks. I have a plan, but I tell nobody. Pip does not know the plan, so Pip does not wait.

He looks at the bird in his hand. “Never again,” he says quietly. “Never again a plan only in my head.”

In the dark Bram looks at him. “Tomas? What?”

Tomas puts the bird under his shirt. “Tomorrow I tell you everything,” he says.

title: The Snare
body:
It is the last night before the sea. The wagon stops in a forest. “Tomorrow we are in the town,” says Odo. “Tomorrow there is money.”

In the evening the men need wood for the fire. Odo opens the cage. “You and you,” he says to Tomas and Bram. “Get wood. The dog goes with you.”

In the forest Tomas collects wood. He also takes the old pieces of rope from under his shirt. On a small path south of the camp he makes snares. Big snares, for men. Next to the path he makes small snares too, for rabbits.

Back in the cage, Tomas tells Bram everything: the plan, the guards, the old man with the wine.

“Tonight the old man watches the cage,” says Tomas. “He drinks, and then he sleeps. His knife is on his belt. I take the knife, and I cut the rope on the door. Then you take the little ones, and you go north. Quietly. All night. Don't stop.”

Bram's face is white. “Me? And you?”

“I take the men south, into the forest. To my snares.”

“I can't, Tomas. I'm not like you.”

“You can. The little ones always listen to you.”

Bram is quiet. Then he says: “OK.”

At night the men sit by the fire and drink wine. Then they sleep. The old man sits near the cage with his wine. Soon his head falls on his chest.

Tomas puts his arm through the bars. Very slowly he takes the knife from the old man's belt. He cuts the rope on the door. The door opens with no sound.

Bram takes the youngest child in his arms. The other little ones hold hands. They go north into the dark. Bram is very afraid, but he goes.

Tomas goes to the horses. He cuts their ropes, and the horses run away into the night.

Then he shouts: “Here! The children are here!” And he runs south.

The men wake up and run after him with the dogs. The first man runs into a snare, and suddenly he hangs from a tree by one foot. In the small snares there are two rabbits now. The dogs smell the rabbits, and they forget Tomas.

Then a big hand takes Tomas by the arm. It is Odo. He is very strong. “You,” he says. “Always you.”

Tomas has the knife. He cuts. The knife goes deep into Odo's hand. Odo cries out, and he lets go.

Tomas runs into the dark. Behind him Odo shouts, but Tomas is already far away.

He runs all night, first south, then east, then north. In the morning he finds the children under a big tree. Bram stands up. His eyes are red, but he smiles.

“All here,” he says. “Five little ones. And me.”

title: The Way Home
body:
The way home is long. The children walk north for many days. They walk at night, and in the day they sleep in the forest.

Tomas makes snares with his old ropes, and every morning there is a rabbit, or two. The children eat berries too. Bram carries the youngest on his back. “Come on!” he says. “Only a little more!” He gives orders again, but now his orders are good.

One night Tomas is awake. Between the trees he sees a light. It is soft and white, and it moves slowly. It is not a fire, and it is not the moon. Then the light is gone.

It is a marsh light, he thinks. Only a marsh light. He tells nobody.

On the twelfth day they see the mountains. Near the monastery there is a very old oak, the oak from Pip's stories. Tomas takes the knife, and in the wood of the oak he writes a name: PIP.

“Pip has no grave,” says Bram. “But here is his name.”

“Now he lives with the King,” says the youngest child.

In the evening the children come to the gate of the monastery. The monks run out. They cry, they laugh, they hold the children. The abbot cries too.

In the dining hall the children eat soup and bread. Bram stands up, and the room is quiet.

“Tomas saved us,” he says. “Not me. Tomas.”

Later, the abbot and Brother Anselm take Tomas to a small room. A candle burns on the table.

“Tomas,” says the abbot. “You were a baby at the gate, like Pip. But you were not there by accident.”

“Somebody left you at our gate,” says Brother Anselm. “With you there was a letter and a ring. The letter is closed with a seal. We promised: we do not open it before you are a man.”

Tomas looks at him. “Who left me?”

Brother Anselm is quiet. “One day you know it, Tomas. Not today.”

In the morning Tomas goes out before the sun is up. He goes to his snares, like always.

On the path there is a rabbit. It is grey, and it has a torn ear. It is the King. The King sits on the path and looks at Tomas. Tomas looks at the King. He puts his hand on the wooden bird under his shirt.

Then the King jumps, and he is gone into the forest.

Far in the south, in a town by the sea, a man with one eye puts a white cloth on his hand. Then he goes to the town hall. He pays a lot of money, and he gets a paper with a big seal. Now he is not a thief. Now he is a merchant.
